summary: This nucleophilic substitution reaction was successfully translated from batch to continuous flow using a PTFE capillary reactor system (1.395 mm ID) with ISCO and Chemyx Nexus pumps. The batch process operated at 115°C for 48 hours achieving 51% yield, while the flow process dramatically increased the temperature to 260°C with only 30 minutes residence time at 18.24 mL/min flow rate, achieving an improved 60% yield. The reaction used n-butanol as solvent with 4-butylimidazole as base, and required a back pressure regulator at 1.0 bar to maintain proper pressure control. Flow chemistry enabled a remarkable 96-fold intensification factor by allowing safe operation at much higher temperatures (260°C vs 115°C) with significantly reduced reaction time (30 min vs 48 h) while improving yield by 9%. The continuous capillary system provided superior heat management and pressure control compared to batch, making the high-temperature conditions safely accessible.

summary: This photoredox catalytic radical substitution uses Ru(bpy)3Cl2 (1 mol%) as photocatalyst to facilitate single electron transfer reactions in acetonitrile at room temperature (25°C). The process was implemented in a microflow reactor using perfluoroalkoxyalkane (PFA) capillary tubing with 0.5 mm internal diameter and 0.5 mL reactor volume, operated at 0.5 mL/min flow rate with blue LED irradiation and 2.76 bar back pressure. The flow system achieved a dramatic 1-minute residence time compared to 60 minutes required in batch, while maintaining 98% yield in both cases. Flow processing provided a 15-fold increase in production rate and enabled a 60-fold reduction in reaction time, while also reducing CF3I reagent usage from 4 equivalents to 1.1 equivalents, addressing safety concerns related to CF3I inventory management.

metadata.mechanism_type: photoredox catalysis with in situ generated catalyst

summary: This photocatalyzed radical addition employs 2-benzopyrylium intermediates generated in situ as the photoredox catalyst under 450 nm LED irradiation. The flow process operates in a 1.0 mL photochemical reactor using 1,2-dichloroethane as solvent at room temperature (25°C) with a 2.5 minute residence time and 24.0 mL/min flow rate, achieving 77% yield. In contrast, the batch baseline required elevated temperature (50°C) and 60 minutes reaction time to obtain 76% yield. Flow processing provided a 24-fold intensification in reaction rate while maintaining comparable yield and enabling safer room temperature operation, demonstrating superior scalability for this photoredox transformation.
